questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: The causes and course of the German hyperinflation of 1921-1923
How the gold standard collapsed across Europe after World War I
How the Dawes Plan was negotiated between Germany and the Allies
The economic recovery of France after the Ruhr occupation
questions.explain: It traces how war debt, reparations and money printing led to Weimar hyperinflation.

questions.q: How did Germany fund World War I, unlike France?
options: By introducing the country's first income tax
By selling overseas colonies to the Allied powers
By shipping its gold reserves to neutral banks
Entirely by borrowing, avoiding new taxes
questions.explain: The Emperor and Reichstag chose to borrow rather than risk angering the public with taxes.

options: French and Belgian troops occupied the Ruhr
The Rentenmark replaced the Papiermark nationwide
Walther Rathenau was assassinated in Berlin
The Dawes Plan restarted reparations payments
questions.explain: After missed coal payments, French and Belgian troops occupied the Ruhr valley.

questions.q: What was the mark's value by November 1923?
options: About 4.2 trillion per dollar
About 7.4 billion per dollar
About 320 million per dollar
About 48 billion per dollar
questions.explain: One US dollar was worth 4,210,500,000,000 marks by November 1923.

questions.q: Why might hyperinflation have benefited the German government?
options: It reduced domestic debts relative to revenues
It raised tax receipts measured in gold marks
It cancelled the reparations owed to the Allies
It improved German exports of coal and timber
questions.explain: Domestic war debts were in paper currency, so inflation greatly reduced them, though reparations were not.
